title: I built a 32-kart Mode 7 racer in Rust with Claude Code: custom engine, browser build, AI-assisted art and audio (free demo)
author: ArthursoftDev
selftext:
**Mega Super Racer** (MSR) is a 90s-inspired arcade kart racer: drifting, boosts, items, up to 32 racers and 4-player split screen. I've just uploaded a free browser demo for desktop and mobile: [https://arthursoft.itch.io/mega-super-racer](https://arthursoft.itch.io/mega-super-racer)

It was built entirely by one dev in their spare time with AI tools in a little over 3 weeks from the initial idea to demo. So as you can imagine, AI did all of the heavy lifting.

I wanted to share some info on the setup, tools and processes I used.

**Engine: custom Rust, with multiple graphics and platform options**

I've been a game developer for 20 years, and in recent years the industry has massively consolidated around a couple of game engines and a handful of technologies. That's been great for productivity, and for having a shared understanding of the tools when moving between projects, but I do miss the days when almost every studio had its own custom tech stack, even if some (most?) of it was super janky!

For MSR I went the custom route, built on a few popular foundations and written in Rust:

* **SDL3 + SDL\_GPU (Vulkan/Metal/D3D12)**, with no off-the-shelf game engine. The ground is a modern take on SNES Mode 7, with fog, parallax skies and sprite-stacked buildings.
* **Server:** (not in the demo; thinking ahead) A pure, deterministic simulation crate: fixed 60 Hz, no IO and no clock, shared by the client, the server and the bots, so adding online play later is a transport job rather than a rewrite.
* **Browser build**: Rust compiled to wasm with Emscripten. Shader compile times in Chrome on Windows with WebGL were painful, so we wrote our own WebGPU and WebGL backends for SDL\_GPU's calls. Shaders go GLSL → SPIR-V → WGSL at build time, which cut the first-load shader compile on Windows Chrome from \~17 s to \~4 s in the demo.

**How I used AI**

Claude Opus 5.5 (mostly on medium effort) has been the backbone of the whole project:

* **Code:** Claude Code with specialist sub-agents (engine, gameplay, tools, netcode, reviewer), each working in its own git worktree, with GitLab CI building Windows, Linux, Android and web on every release. I provide the design and the taste; the agents write, test and screenshot their own changes.
* **Art:** PixelLab made all of the character and kart sprites, with a few manual touch-ups in Aseprite. The tracks are painted by our own generator from splines, and most of the track textures and buildings were generated directly by Claude through Rust or Python tools.
* **Music:** I started with Suno, which is incredible, but I struggled to get that 90s MIDI feel that I was looking for. Then I came across SuperCollider, a programmable environment for making audio algorithmically. With a few instrument packs, SuperCollider and Opus 5.5 on high effort (sometimes Fable 5.1), we produced all of the music in the game and I genuinely think some of it is really good!
* **Sound:** SFX and engine loops come from a small synth tool Claude wrote, and the character voices are cartoon gibberish from another Claude-built tool. I'm not super happy with these yet, so I'll be trying some other options soon.
* **Translations:** Claude has auto translated the game into 6 languages from English. I don't speak *any* of them, so it could be total nonsense, but I wanted the pipeline in place.

**What didn't work / lessons**

* Claude is terrible at making art directly (attempts were made at "pixel art"), but it is really good at using tools, and pretty damn good at building simple geometric models, which came in really handy for building up the game's environments.
* Claude *really* likes tests but tests break constantly as you develop, and you eventually reach a point where all of your compute goes on running tests, checking the broken tests, finding out the broken tests were themselves not right, fixing the broken tests, then running all again. I had to ask Claude to streamline the tests several times because it was slowing the process down massively, especially in CI (the same tests ran on commit, before a merge and again after it). Sure, you could throw more hardware at the problem but I'm a game developer - that's not how I was raised!
* Browser quirks ate days: Safari's shader compiler, Mac Chrome's WebGPU running at 10 fps, and iPhone having no fullscreen for web pages.

Happy to answer questions about the pipeline. Feedback on the demo is very welcome, and we're on Discord too: [https://discord.gg/kHeEgGdGmf](https://discord.gg/kHeEgGdGmf)

comments.author: Sacred_B
comments.body: Really curious on how you handle planning and breakout of the workload between agents. Did you plan out your whole dev process using like KANBAN, then just tackle it one subagent per story?  Did you plan as you go? Did you lean into Claude for any sort of design choice planning/critique?

replies.author: ArthursoftDev
replies.body:
I've been in game development for nearly 20 years now (mostly AAA dev) and seen a lot of different processes, kanban, scrum, sprints, waterfall (lots and lots of waterfall 😅), but honestly I didn't find any of that to be a good fit in this case. They're all processes designed in some way shape or form to gather requirements and communicate those across team and stakeholders. 

That's ok when you're working with people, makes it organises, when working in AI Agents though, I just find that to be paperwork for paperwork's sake. At the end of the day it sort of just becomes an expensive record of decisions, which could be captured in more efficient ways anyway.

This was much more adhoc, fluid and iterative. I had an initial idea from a previous test project I had been working on which formed the plan. I iterated on that plan with Claude to form a short design brief, set of criteria and rules and then just started building, fast. Think we had 8 courses, all 16 characters, some power-ups and 4 player split screen roughed out in the first afternoon and from their we simply iterated across every aspect of the game, building tools as we went along and constantly play testing.

That probably sounds a bit hectic, but then I've been doing this professionally for for decades and it certainly hasn't been as hectic as some titles I've worked on!

comments.author: Wavertron
comments.body: If AI is writing the bulk of the code, why bother with unit tests?

replies.author: ArthursoftDev
replies.body:
You know, it's funny you should say that as I just had a conversation earlier this week with a Tech Director who said precisely the opposite "One of the great things about AI writing code, is it writes Unit tests that most of us coders forget to get around to writing".

Unit tests *are* useful, but having too many and running them too often just grinds things to a super slow pace. We have a lot of really helpful tests in place that help with difficulty balancing, pick up probabilities, checking handling changes, performance testing, language changes.

I agree with the Tech Director, why *wouldn't* you use unit tests when AI writes the bulk of the code.

replies.author: Wavertron
replies.body:
I  guess my concern would be if the AI is generating tests by looking at the code and the branches in logic, that it becomes a kind of self-referential correctness that wont necessarily catch any bugs because it wont be reasoning about expected behaviour like a human would.

Or have you found the quality of tests really good?  
Do you have to prompt it on the test cases you want, particularly more subtle scenarios?

replies.author: freqCake
replies.body:
It is not about catching bugs, it is about catching changes in behaviour globally given any change (by re-running the suite every change) and forcing it into the model's context allowing it to reason about what, how, and why its change has impacted behaviour and surface the impacts of changes (To you).

"This change made rendering change in 2d scenes"

Not

"This change made the rendering wrong for 2d scenes"

replies.author: Wavertron
replies.body: Yeah fair point, not unlike when we humans make changes.

comments.author: Wavertron
comments.body: If AI is writing the bulk of the code, why bother with unit tests?

replies.author: Bubbly_Donkey_8538
replies.body: This is one of the dumbest things I've read recently

replies.author: freqCake
replies.body:
As ai makes changes to the code the unit tests provide automated regression checks which enforce alerts when behaviour has changed.

Even if the original behaviour being tested for was unintended, this aids the model in having context for what a change in one area has changed in other areas.

replies.author: Bubbly_Donkey_8538
replies.body: You clearly have no idea how LLMs work.

replies.author: Bubbly_Donkey_8538
replies.body: u/askgrok In a vibe coding project why bothering writing unit tests

replies.author: AskGrok
replies.body:
Because in vibe coding the AI hallucinates, refactors break determinism, and one bad merge can nuke the whole 60 Hz sim. Tests are the only thing that keeps the "vibes" from turning into unplayable jank when you iterate 50 times a day. The dev in the post learned the hard way they slow everything down though, so most people just skip or slim them hard for prototypes.

^([what is this?](https://redd.it/1lzgxii))
